# FadeCurve

[Framework](README.md) · `DotGame.Framework.Audio` · class

```csharp
public abstract class FadeCurve
```

The shape a volume fade follows over its duration.

## Remarks

A curve describes only the shape of a fade, on normalized progress from 0 (the moment the fade starts) to 1 (the moment it ends). It is applied the same way whether the volume is rising or falling, so a single instance serves both fade-ins and fade-outs.

The built-in curves are [`Linear`](#linear), [`Exponential`](#exponential), [`Sine`](#sine), and [`SCurve`](#scurve). Custom shapes are supported: derive from this class and implement [`InterpolateCore`](#interpolatecore). A custom curve works on every platform, including the browser, because the shape is always evaluated by this managed code.

Instances must be immutable and safe to share; a single instance is typically reused for the lifetime of the game.

## Properties

### Exponential

```csharp
public static FadeCurve Exponential { get; }
```

A constant-decibel fade, and the default for [`VolumeControl.FadeTo`](VolumeControl.md#fadeto).

The volume follows from * (to / from) ^ t, which is a constant number of decibels per second and is therefore perceived as changing at a steady rate rather than dropping away abruptly at the end of a fade-out.

### Linear

```csharp
public static FadeCurve Linear { get; }
```

A constant-amplitude fade: the volume value changes at a steady rate.

Because perceived loudness is logarithmic, a linear amplitude fade sounds like it holds its level for most of the fade and then falls off a cliff at the very end. It is included for cases where the mathematical shape matters more than the perceived one.

### SCurve

```csharp
public static FadeCurve SCurve { get; }
```

A symmetric fade that eases at both ends: it leaves the starting level gradually, moves fastest through the middle, and settles gently onto the target.

The flat start means the fade takes a moment to become audible, which is what makes it feel unobtrusive for long transitions such as a scene change or a music swap. For the same reason it is a poor fit for short fades like ducking, where the delay reads as lag; prefer [`Sine`](#sine) or [`Exponential`](#exponential) there.

### Sine

```csharp
public static FadeCurve Sine { get; }
```

A sine quarter-wave fade, which moves away from the starting level immediately and eases gently into the target.

A single instance covers both directions: a falling fade through this curve produces the mirrored (cosine) shape, so no separate curve is needed for fading out. Two tracks cross-faded with this curve hold a near-constant combined power -- it is the equal-power cross-fade -- which is what makes it the usual choice for swapping one track for another.

## Methods

### InterpolateCore

```csharp
protected abstract float InterpolateCore(float fromVolume, float toVolume, float t)
```

Computes the volume at normalized fade progress `t`.

| Parameter | |
|---|---|
| `fromVolume` | The volume at the start of the fade. |
| `toVolume` | The volume at the end of the fade. |
| `t` | Fade progress, strictly between 0 and 1 exclusive. |

The endpoints are handled by `Interpolate` and are never passed here, so an implementation only has to describe the shape in between and need not special-case t = 0 or t = 1.
